### Definition (Power System Bus)
A **bus** (or **busbar**) in a power system is a **node/junction** where one or more elements are electrically connected—such as **generators, loads, transmission lines, transformers, shunt capacitors/reactors**.  
All points on a bus are assumed to have the **same voltage magnitude and phase angle** (i.e., it is treated as a single node in power-flow studies).

---

## Classification of Buses (with examples)

### 1) **Slack (Swing / Reference) Bus**
**Definition:**  
A bus at which **voltage magnitude \(|V|\)** and **voltage angle \(\delta\)** are specified.  
It **balances the system power** by supplying/absorbing the mismatch in real and reactive power (covers losses and modeling mismatch).

**Specified:** \(|V|\), \(\delta\)  
**Unknown (solved):** \(P\), \(Q\)

**Why needed:**  
Power-flow equations need one reference angle and one bus to take up net power imbalance.

**Example:**  
- In a 3-bus system, **Bus 1** is connected to a strong grid/generator and is set to:  
  \[
  |V_1| = 1.04\ pu,\quad \delta_1 = 0^\circ
  \]
  Then the load-flow solution computes the actual \(P_1\) and \(Q_1\) generated to meet total demand + losses.

**Typical practical case:**  
- A large generating station bus or interconnection to an infinite bus (grid) chosen as reference.

---

### 2) **PV Bus (Generator / Voltage-Controlled Bus)**
**Definition:**  
A bus where a **generator is connected** and it regulates voltage using excitation control.  
Here **real power \(P\)** and **voltage magnitude \(|V|\)** are specified.

**Specified:** \(P\), \(|V|\)  
**Unknown (solved):** \(\delta\), \(Q\)

**Reactive power limits:**  
If computed \(Q\) violates generator limits \((Q_{\min}, Q_{\max})\), the bus is typically converted to a **PQ bus** with \(Q\) fixed at the limit.

**Example:**  
- **Bus 2** has a generator scheduled at:
  \[
  P_2 = 80\ \text{MW},\quad |V_2| = 1.01\ pu
  \]
  Load flow finds \(\delta_2\) and the required \(Q_2\) to hold 1.01 pu.

**Typical practical case:**  
- Generator terminal bus in transmission system where AVR maintains voltage.

---

### 3) **PQ Bus (Load Bus)**
**Definition:**  
A bus where **load demand** is specified. Both **real and reactive power** are given.

**Specified:** \(P\), \(Q\) (load demand, usually negative injection)  
**Unknown (solved):** \(|V|\), \(\delta\)

**Example:**  
- **Bus 3** supplies a load:
  \[
  P_3 = 100\ \text{MW},\quad Q_3 = 60\ \text{MVAr}
  \]
  Load flow computes \(|V_3|\) and \(\delta_3\).

**Typical practical case:**  
- Distribution substation bus feeding mixed loads, or any non-voltage-controlled load point.

---

## Summary Table

| Bus Type | Also Called | Specified | Solved/Unknown | Typical Use |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Slack | Swing/Reference | \(|V|,\ \delta\) | \(P,\ Q\) | Reference + loss balance |
| PV | Generator/Voltage-controlled | \(P,\ |V|\) | \(\delta,\ Q\) (within limits) | Generator bus with AVR |
| PQ | Load bus | \(P,\ Q\) | \(|V|,\ \delta\) | Load/substation bus |

---

If you want, I can also provide a **complete numeric 3-bus example** (line data + Y-bus + final solved voltages) showing how each bus type is used in a load-flow study.
